facts.fact_text: In 2006 the applicant, together with other individuals, organised a march to draw public attention to discrimination against the gay and lesbian minority in Russia.
The march organised in 2006 aimed to promote respect for human rights and freedoms.
The march organised in 2006 aimed to call for tolerance on the part of the Russian authorities and the public at large towards the gay and lesbian minority.
The intended march was to take place between 3 p.m. and 5 p.m. on 27 May 2006.
The intended march had an estimated number of about 2,000 participants.
The organisers of the Pride March undertook to cooperate with the law-enforcement authorities in ensuring safety and respect for public order by the participants.
The organisers informed the prefect of their intention to hold a picket in the park at Lubyanskaya Square on 27 May 2006.

At the conference celebrating the International Day Against Homophobia on 27 May 2006, the applicant and several other persons announced their intention to gather in the Aleksandrovskiy Garden to lay flowers at the war memorial, the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, allegedly to commemorate the victims of fascism, including gay and lesbian victims.

At the conference celebrating the International Day Against Homophobia on 27 May 2006, the applicant and several other persons announced their intention to hold a fifteen-minute picket at the Moscow mayor's office to protest against the ban on the march and the picketing.

On 26 May 2007 the applicant and several other persons announced at the annual 'LGBT Rights are Human Rights' conference that they would meet the following day in front of the Moscow mayor's office to file a petition together in protest against the ban on the march and the picketing.
On 1 June 2008 the applicant, in a group of twenty individuals, held a picket on Bolshaya Nikitskaya Street for about ten minutes.
Mr Tsoy, the press secretary of the mayor of Moscow, stated that the government of Moscow would not even consider allowing the gay parade to be held.
Mr Tsoy stated that any attempt to hold any unauthorised action would be severely repressed.
On 18 May 2006 the Department for Liaison with Security Authorities of the Moscow Government informed the applicant of the mayor's decision to refuse permission to hold the march.
The mayor of Moscow refused permission to hold the Pride March on grounds of public order, for the prevention of riots and the protection of health, morals and the rights and freedoms of others.
On 23 May 2006 the deputy prefect of the Moscow Central Administrative Circuit refused permission to hold the picket at Lubyanskaya Square.
The deputy prefect of the Moscow Central Administrative Circuit refused permission to hold the picket on the same grounds as those given for the refusal to hold the Pride March.

On 16 May 2007 the Department for Liaison with Security Authorities of the Moscow Government informed the applicant that permission to hold the 2007 march had been refused on the grounds of potential breaches of public order and violence against the participants, with reference to the events of the previous year.

On 23 May 2007 the organisers were informed that the prefect had refused permission to hold the picket at Tverskaya Square on grounds of public order, prevention of riots and protection of health, morals and the rights and freedoms of others.

On 23 May 2007 the organisers were informed that the prefect had refused permission to hold the picket in Novopushkinskiy Park on grounds of public order, prevention of riots and protection of health, morals and the rights and freedoms of others.

On 24 April 2008 the Department for Liaison with Security Authorities of the Moscow Government informed the applicant that permission to hold all ten marches planned for 1 and 2 May 2008 had been refused on the grounds of potential breaches of public order and violence against the participants.

On 28 April 2008 the Department for Liaison with Security Authorities of the Moscow Government informed the applicant that permission to hold the fifteen marches planned from 3 to 5 May 2008 had been refused on the same grounds as the previous refusals.
The applicant submitted applications dated 25 and 28 April 2008 for 30 marches in total, which were refused on 5 May 2008 on the same grounds as previous refusals.
The applicant submitted an application dated 30 April 2008 for 20 marches, which was refused on 7 May 2008 on the same grounds as previous refusals.
The applicant submitted an application dated 5 May 2008 for 20 marches, which was refused on 8 May 2008 on the same grounds as previous refusals.
The applicant submitted an application dated 8 May 2008 for 15 marches, which was refused on 13 May 2008 on the same grounds as previous refusals.
The applicant submitted an application dated 12 May 2008 for 15 marches, which was refused on 16 May 2008 on the same grounds as previous refusals.
The applicant submitted an application dated 15 May 2008 for 15 marches, which was refused on 21 May 2008 on the same grounds as previous refusals.
The applicant submitted an application dated 19 May 2008 for 15 marches, which was refused on 23 May 2008 on the same grounds as previous refusals.
The picket intended to be held on 17 May 2008 was prohibited on 13 May 2008 on the same grounds as those given for the previous events.

Article 55 § 3 of the Constitution of the Russian Federation provides that rights and freedoms may be restricted by federal laws for the protection of constitutional principles, public morals, health and the rights and lawful interests of others, and to ensure the defence and security of the State.

Section 5(3)(i) of the Federal Law on Assemblies, Meetings, Demonstrations, Marches and Picketing (no. 54-FZ of 18 August 2004, the Assemblies Act) provides that the organiser of a public event has the right to hold meetings, demonstrations, marches and pickets at the venues and time specified in the notice on holding the public event or as altered by agreement with the executive authority of the subject of the Russian Federation or the municipal body.

Section 5(4)(i) of the Assemblies Act provides that the organiser of the public event must submit to the executive authority of the subject of the Russian Federation or the municipal body a notice on holding the public event in accordance with the procedure prescribed by section 7 of the Assemblies Act.

Section 5(4)(ii) of the Assemblies Act provides that the organiser of the public event must, no later than three days prior to the holding of the public event, notify in writing the executive authority of the subject of the Russian Federation or the municipal body of the acceptance or non-acceptance of its proposal to alter the venue and/or time of the public event as specified in the notice of the event.

Section 5(4)(iii) of the Assemblies Act provides that the organiser of the public event must ensure compliance with the conditions for holding the public event as specified in the notice of the event or with any conditions that have been altered as a result of an agreement reached with the executive authority of the subject of the Russian Federation or the municipal body.

Section 5(4)(iv) of the Assemblies Act provides that the organiser of the public event must require the participants in the public event to observe public order and comply with the conditions for holding the public event, and that persons who fail to comply with the lawful requirements of the organiser may be expelled from the venue.

Section 5(5) of the Assemblies Act provides that the organiser of the public event shall have no right to hold it if the notice on holding the public event has not been submitted in due time or no agreement has been reached with the executive authority of the subject of the Russian Federation or the municipal body on their reasoned proposal as to the alteration of the venue and/or time of the public event.

Section 8 of the Assemblies Act provides that a public event may be held at any venue suitable for holding the event if its conduct does not create a threat of the collapse of buildings or structures or other threats to the safety of the participants in the public event.
Section 8 of the Assemblies Act provides that conditions governing bans or restrictions on holding a public event at particular venues may be specified by federal laws.

Section 12(1)(ii) of the Assemblies Act provides that the executive authority of the subject of the Russian Federation or the municipal body, upon receiving notice of the public event, must inform the organiser of the public event, within three days of receipt of the notice, of a reasoned proposal to alter the venue and/or time of the public event, as well as of any proposal for the organiser to bring the aims, form or other conditions for holding the event into line with the requirements of the Assemblies Act.

Section 12(1)(iii) of the Assemblies Act provides that the executive authority of the subject of the Russian Federation or the municipal body must designate, depending on the form of the public event and the number of participants, an authorised representative to assist the event organisers in conducting the event in accordance with the Assemblies Act.

Section 12(1)(v) of the Assemblies Act provides that the executive authority of the subject of the Russian Federation or the municipal body must ensure, within its competence and jointly with the organiser of the public event and the authorised representative of the Ministry of the Interior, public order and safety of citizens while holding the event and, if necessary, provide them with urgent medical aid.
Section 14(3)(i) of the Assemblies Act provides that the authorised representative of the Ministry of the Interior must facilitate the conduct of the public event.

Section 14(3)(ii) of the Assemblies Act provides that the authorised representative of the Ministry of the Interior must ensure, jointly with the organiser of the public event and the executive authority of the subject of the Russian Federation or the municipal body, public order and safety of citizens and compliance with the law while holding the public event.

Section 18(1) of the Assemblies Act provides that the organiser of the public event, officials or other individuals may not prevent the participants in the event from expressing their opinion in a manner that does not breach public order or the conditions for holding the public event.
The mayor of Moscow refused permission to hold the Pride March on grounds of public order, for the prevention of riots and the protection of health, morals and the rights and freedoms of others.
The mayor of Moscow stated he would ban a gay parade because he did not want to stir up society, which is ill-disposed to such occurrences of life.
The first deputy to the mayor of Moscow considered that allowing the gay parade event would be contrary to health and morals.

The Department for Liaison with Security Authorities of the Moscow Government stated that numerous petitions had been brought against the march by representatives of legislative and executive State bodies, religious denominations, Cossack elders and other individuals.

The Department for Liaison with Security Authorities of the Moscow Government stated that the march was likely to cause a negative reaction and protests against the participants, which could turn into civil disorder and mass riots.

On 23 May 2007 the organisers were informed that the prefect had refused permission to hold the picket at Tverskaya Square on grounds of public order, prevention of riots and protection of health, morals and the rights and freedoms of others.

On 23 May 2007 the organisers were informed that the prefect had refused permission to hold the picket in Novopushkinskiy Park on grounds of public order, prevention of riots and protection of health, morals and the rights and freedoms of others.

On 24 August 2007 the Taganskiy District Court of Moscow dismissed the complaint concerning the ban on the picketing planned for 27 May 2007, finding that the ban had been justified on safety grounds.
The Taganskiy District Court judgment of 24 August 2007 was upheld on 8 November 2007 by the Moscow City Court.
The decision prohibiting the picket intended for 17 May 2008 was reviewed and upheld by the Taganskiy District Court on 22 July 2008.
The decision prohibiting the picket intended for 17 May 2008 was upheld on appeal by the Moscow City Court on 14 October 2008.
The mayor of Moscow stated that he himself considered homosexuality 'unnatural', though he tried to treat everything that happens in human society with tolerance.
The mayor of Moscow stated that the gay parade was absolutely unacceptable in Moscow and in Russia, unlike in some Western countries more progressive in that sphere.

The mayor of Moscow stated: 'That's the way morals work. If somebody deviates from the normal principles [in accordance with which] sexual and gender life is organised, this should not be demonstrated in public and anyone potentially unstable should not be invited.'

The Tverskoy District Court of Moscow considered that the refusal to hold the Pride March had legitimate grounds and that the applicant's right to hold assemblies and other public events had not been breached.

Recommendation CM/Rec(2010)5 of the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe to member States, paragraph 16, provides that member states should take appropriate measures to prevent restrictions on the effective enjoyment of the rights to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly resulting from the abuse of legal or administrative provisions, for example on grounds of public health, public morality and public order.

Recommendation CM/Rec(2010)5 of the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe to member States, paragraph 14, provides that member states should take appropriate measures at national, regional and local levels to ensure that the right to freedom of peaceful assembly can be effectively enjoyed, without discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.

Section 12(1)(v) of the Assemblies Act provides that the executive authority of the subject of the Russian Federation or the municipal body must ensure, within its competence and jointly with the organiser of the public event and the authorised representative of the Ministry of the Interior, public order and safety of citizens while holding the event and, if necessary, provide them with urgent medical aid.

Section 14(3)(ii) of the Assemblies Act provides that the authorised representative of the Ministry of the Interior must ensure, jointly with the organiser of the public event and the executive authority of the subject of the Russian Federation or the municipal body, public order and safety of citizens and compliance with the law while holding the public event.

Recommendation CM/Rec(2010)5 of the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe to member States, paragraph 15, provides that member states should ensure that law enforcement authorities take appropriate measures to protect participants in peaceful demonstrations in favour of the human rights of lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender persons from any attempts to unlawfully disrupt or inhibit the effective enjoyment of their right to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly.

In a statement given in St Petersburg on 5 June 2006, Commissioner Hammarberg stressed that the rights to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly belong to all people and that the authorities have a duty to protect peaceful demonstrators.
